what: Solaris Energy Infrastructure supplies mobile power generation. It owns fleets of turbines and engines that it leases to customers who need electricity quickly where the grid cannot supply it — increasingly data centres. It also runs the sand silo and proppant management equipment business it was originally built on.
customers: Data centre developers and operators needing power before a grid connection is available, plus oil and gas operators needing power and sand handling at well sites.
money: Leasing mobile turbines and generating equipment, increasingly on multi-year contracts to data centres.
Sand silos, proppant and chemical handling systems for hydraulic fracturing.
moat: The scarce thing is not the equipment but the position: a large turbine fleet that can be delivered and running in months, at a moment when grid connection queues run for years. Turbine manufacturing slots are themselves sold out well into the future, so owning fleet today is a genuine advantage, and multi-year leases to creditworthy data centre customers turn it into contracted revenue.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $1.1B in the trailing period: the company is buying turbines far faster than the leases pay for them.
The shares trade at about 64 times earnings and 21 times EV/EBITDA, which already prices in years of successful expansion.

This advantage is explicitly temporary. It exists because grid connections are slow and turbines are scarce; both of those ease over time, and when they do, mobile power becomes an ordinary rental business.
The legacy sand-handling business is tied to hydraulic fracturing activity, which is cyclical and currently soft.
Fourteen analysts average a $107.77 target against a $61.43 price. A 75% gap on a company consuming over a billion dollars of cash is a forecast of contracts, not of results.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $313.1M in 2024 to $622.2M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $936.4M.
Data centre developers will pay a great deal to start earning revenue years before a grid connection arrives, which is exactly what this equipment lets them do.
Debt of $194.4M against $353.3M of cash is modest, so the expansion has so far been funded without heavy borrowing.
Each turbine placed on a multi-year contract converts a capital purchase into predictable revenue for the length of that contract.
watch: Contracted megawatts and the length of the contracts. The equipment is only worth what someone has agreed to pay for it over time, and that figure is what separates this from a rental company with a lot of idle turbines.
view: This is a bet on a bottleneck, and bottleneck bets have a specific shape: enormous returns while the bottleneck lasts, ordinary returns the moment it clears. Right now the bottleneck is electricity. A data centre developer can finance and build a facility far faster than a utility can connect it to the grid, and an unconnected data centre earns nothing. Solaris owns turbines it can deliver and run in months, and developers will pay a great deal for that gap to be filled. That is the whole story, and it is a good one.

What the market is paying for it is 64 times earnings and 21 times EV/EBITDA, while the company burns $1.1 billion of cash a year buying more turbines. That burn is not a warning sign in itself — it is a company buying revenue-generating assets as fast as it can get them, which is the right move when demand exceeds supply. But it does mean the balance sheet and the contract book matter far more than the income statement. The $194 million of debt against $353 million of cash is reassuring today; the question is how the next billion of turbines gets funded.

The part I would think hardest about is what happens on the other side. Turbine manufacturers are expanding. Utilities are working through connection queues. Both will take years, which is why this works for now, but neither is permanent. When grid power catches up, mobile generation reverts to being an equipment rental business, and equipment rental businesses do not trade at 64 times earnings. The company’s answer — lock the fleet into multi-year contracts while the scarcity lasts — is the right one, and it is why contracted megawatts and contract duration are the only numbers I would track.

So: a real asset in a real shortage, run by people who are moving fast, at a price that assumes the shortage persists long enough to pay for the fleet several times over. The fourteen analysts at $107.77 are underwriting exactly that. I would treat this as a cyclical dressed as a growth company — which is what equipment businesses in a shortage always are — and I would want to know the weighted average remaining contract life before paying this multiple. If it is five years, the case is strong. If it is eighteen months, you are renting turbines to a boom.
bull: Grid connection queues stay long, every new turbine goes onto a multi-year contract with a creditworthy data centre customer, and the fleet pays for itself several times before supply catches up.
bear: Turbine supply and grid connections both ease, the fleet comes off contract into an ordinary rental market, and 64 times earnings meets a cash-hungry equipment business.
